What if Africa’s energy challenge is not only about who gets connected, but what those connections make possible?

That was the reflection I took from yesterday’s discussion on “From Evidence to Action: Accelerating Energy Access and Just Transitions in Africa,” hosted at the Permanent Representation of Nigeria.

Electricity access in sub-Saharan Africa rose from 51% in 2017 to 61% in 2023, with more than 120 million people gaining access in six years. Yet the scale of the challenge remains stark: the region still accounts for 86% of the global electricity access deficit, with 563 million people without power, while around 970 million people lack clean cooking.

The message from today was clear: energy access must become a platform for jobs, resilience, industry and a just transition.

Africa has the resources to lead this shift. The continent holds around 60% of the world’s best solar resources and more than 30% of known critical mineral reserves, yet imports over 80% of the technologies needed for renewable energy deployment. The opportunity is to turn this potential into cheaper power, local value chains, clean industries and decent jobs.

Decentralized energy systems are central to this agenda, especially in hard-to-reach communities.

Through initiatives Africa Minigrids Programme, Energy for Grwoth and Solar for Healts, and collaborating with Mission 300 partners, UNDP is helping African countries move beyond isolated pilot projects by creating the enabling environment for renewable energy system to scale through commercial investment, rural electrification and productive energy use.

Delivery must also become smarter. AI-enabled grid management can improve renewable integration by 20–30%, while geospatial planning, as seen in Rwanda, Zambia and Nigeria, can target grid, mini-grid and off-grid solutions where they best support rural electrification, agriculture, healthcare and local enterprise.

Africa’s energy future is not defined by a lack of potential, but by how quickly we can turn evidence into investment, and investment into delivery that creates jobs, strengthens local enterprise and expands shared prosperity.
